enrichment.short_title: Planning s288 appeal over utility room extension
key_facts: Mr Williams, acting in person, appealed under section 288 against an inspector's dismissal of his planning appeal for a utility laundry and amended roof at Greenacres, Northallerton.
Hambleton District Council had refused planning permission for the extension to a dwelling for which permission had already been granted.
The claimant argued the inspector erred over a 70% versus 57% size comparison, visual impact, form of the extension, and procedural unfairness over local precedents.
The inspector corrected the 70% figure as a typographical error in a witness statement and Gibbs J accepted he had relied on 57%.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory challenge under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to a planning inspector's appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; agreed costs of £2,363.75 awarded to the Secretary of State.
enrichment.ratio: A typographical error in an inspector's decision does not invalidate the decision if the inspector's sworn witness statement shows the reasoning rested on the correct figure; assessments of visual impact and architectural form are matters for the inspector unless no reasonable inspector could have reached the conclusion, and an inspector may lawfully decline to give weight to local precedents while still having regard to representations made.
legal_issues: Whether an inspector's 70% size comparison error rendered the decision unlawful
Wednesbury review of visual impact and form assessments
Procedural fairness where an inspector indicated precedents would not be considered
Summary assessment of costs following partial concession by the Treasury Solicitor

confidence.notes: Full first-instance judgment with clearly reasoned grounds of appeal and explicit dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: Strike-out of negligence counterclaim for CPR non-compliance
key_facts: Miss Patel counterclaimed against Irwin Mitchell Solicitors for alleged negligence in her Employment Tribunal unfair dismissal claim, seeking over £173,000.

Irwin Mitchell applied without properly serving Miss Patel for copies of disclosed documents and a schedule of loss; a district judge treated the application as without notice and made an automatic unless order.
Miss Patel's defence and counterclaim were struck out on 1 October 2001 after she wrote urgently to the court but before her correspondence was treated as an application to vary the order.
His Honour Judge Reynolds QC dismissed her appeal as out of time; the Court of Appeal set aside the underlying orders and remitted the case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal against county court orders striking out a litigant in person's defence and counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; time extended, strike-out and related orders set aside, and case remitted to the Central London County Court for a case management conference.
enrichment.ratio: An unless order made on the basis of a mischaracterised without-notice application that was never served on the defendant cannot stand, and a judge who refuses to treat urgent correspondence raising the merits as an application to vary or set aside such an order fails the justice required under the overriding objective and authorities such as Biguzzi v Rank Leisure Plc.
legal_issues: Validity of an unless order made without proper service of the underlying application
Whether correspondence to the court can stop time running under an unless order
Relief against sanction under CPR 3.9 and reinstatement of pleadings
Extension of time for appeal where procedural unfairness caused prejudice

confidence.notes: Detailed Court of Appeal judgment with explicit order setting aside multiple lower court orders.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum subsistence reduction and 72% income support policy
key_facts: Mrs Gjini, a Kosovan asylum seeker with her son Mario, challenged Islington Council's May 2000 decision to reduce subsistence by deducting £15 per week child benefit.
The council's policy treated asylum support as 72% of income support rates less child benefit, with additional benefits in kind including accommodation and utility bills.
Owen J dismissed judicial review, finding the 72% policy had not been satisfactorily explained but was not shown to have been applied, and upholding the £3 per day family rate and adequacy review.
By the appeal hearing the council had revised its policy and increased payments; the appellant pursued only whether the old 72% policy had been properly applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of an application for judicial review of a local authority asylum subsistence decision.
enrichment.ratio: Where a judicial review claimant abandoned or succeeded on the rationality of a subsistence policy and the judge held the policy either did not exist or would have been irrational if applied, it is unjust to allow a new argument on appeal that the council failed to apply that policy on the assumption it was lawful; inadequate pleading and evidence at first instance may also preclude the point.
legal_issues: Rationality of deducting child benefit from asylum subsistence payments
Lawfulness of a 72% of income support subsistence policy
Whether the council properly applied its subsistence policy to Mrs Gjini
Duty of full and frank disclosure on ex parte permission applications

confidence.notes: Complex procedural history but clear appellate reasoning on the narrow surviving issue.

enrichment.short_title: Disapplying defamation limitation for related slanders
key_facts: Mr Maccaba sued Rabbi Dayan Lichtenstein for nine alleged slanders, harassment, and breach of confidence arising from disputes within the orthodox Jewish community.
Two alleged slanders in January and February 2001 were issued more than one year before proceedings commenced and were otherwise time-barred under section 4A.
The same factual allegations remained live in a six-year harassment claim and seven in-time slander claims, with overlapping defences of justification and qualified privilege.
The claimant had sought redress through the Beth Din and Conference of European Rabbis before issuing High Court proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application under section 32A of the Limitation Act 1980 to disapply the one-year defamation limitation period for two claims.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; section 4A disapplied in relation to the two time-barred slander claims.
enrichment.ratio: Section 32A requires exceptional cases and an equitable balance of prejudice; where delay is very short, evidence remains cogent, the defendant knew of the complaints, the action will proceed in any event on related causes, and excising two slanders from a multi-publication campaign would be artificial before a jury, disapplication may be justified even without a full explanation for the delay.
legal_issues: Exercise of discretion under section 32A Limitation Act 1980
Prejudice in multi-publication defamation and harassment claims
Effect of pursuing religious community remedies before litigation
Whether merits should be tried on a limitation application

confidence.notes: Detailed limitation judgment with explicit grant of the section 32A application.

enrichment.short_title: Offshore pipelaying patent revoked for obviousness
key_facts: Rockwater sought revocation of European Patent (UK) 0 478 742 relating to vertically unrolling flexible tubular conduits from a vessel.
Coflexip and Technip counterclaimed that Rockwater's pipelaying vessel Toisa Perseus infringed apparatus claims used on Leadon and East Foinaven contracts in 2001.
Coflexip accepted Rockwater had not infringed the process claims and relied on hardware capable of operating the patented process.

Laddie J held the Toisa Perseus did not infringe because downstream guide means meant the tensioners were not the last means for guiding the conduit, and the patent was invalid for obviousness over Recalde prior art.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Patent revocation action with counterclaim for infringement in the Patents Court.
enrichment.outcome: Rockwater succeeded on both non-infringement and invalidity; the patent claims failed.
enrichment.ratio: In apparatus claims requiring a tensioner to comprise the last means for guiding flexible conduit on board the vessel, downstream guide structures such as a flared device prevent infringement; and where Recalde prior art discloses the same hardware and obvious modifications would achieve the claimed process, the patent lacks inventive step.
legal_issues: Construction of 'last means for guiding the flexible conduit'
Infringement of apparatus claims where only capability, not actual use, is alleged
Obviousness over Recalde US and Recalde GB prior art
Relationship between process and apparatus claims after Stolt litigation

confidence.notes: Very long technical judgment; core holdings on claim 3 construction and Recalde obviousness are explicit at the end.

enrichment.short_title: Quashing s73 certificate after fresh psychiatric evidence
key_facts: Mr Soylemez, a Turkish Kurdish asylum seeker, had his asylum appeal dismissed after the adjudicator found his torture and detention claims incredible.
Fresh psychiatric reports from Dr Pierzchniak diagnosed PTSD and depression linked to alleged torture and warned of catastrophic deterioration and suicide risk if removed to Turkey.
The Secretary of State refused further representations and certified under section 73(8) that the application had no legitimate purpose other than delay.
Davis J applied the Vemenac test that certification requires the claim to be hopeless or manifestly unfounded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a section 73(8) certificate removing the right of appeal against a post-determination human rights application.
enrichment.outcome: Certificate quashed; claimant entitled to appeal to an adjudicator.
enrichment.ratio: Even where an adjudicator has rejected a claimant's torture account, fresh psychiatric evidence of PTSD and a strongly expressed suicide risk on return may be significant and credible enough that the Secretary of State cannot reasonably certify the further human rights application as manifestly unfounded under section 73(8).
legal_issues: Lawfulness of certification under section 73(8) Immigration and Asylum Act 1999
Effect of fresh medical evidence after a failed asylum appeal
Article 2 and Article 3 ECHR protection against removal
Whether the Secretary of State may reject adjudicator findings without new material

confidence.notes: Long judgment but explicit quashing of the section 73(8) certificate.

enrichment.short_title: Equal pay burden of proof for TUPE pay gap

statutes_considered.title: Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 1981

key_facts: Mrs Nelson, a female steward at Chelsea and Westminster Hospital, was paid less than male comparator Mr d'Silva doing like work.
Transferred Initial Healthcare employees retained higher TUPE-protected pay, meal allowances, and bank holiday terms; later recruits were on the employer's standard terms.
The employer relied on section 1(3), arguing the pay variation was due to TUPE obligations rather than sex.
The appellant contended indirect sex discrimination from statistics showing 80% of retained men but only 66.66% of retained women could comply with the TUPE-based higher pay condition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of an equal pay claim.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 1(3) of the Equal Pay Act 1970 the employer must prove the absence of sex discrimination, but in an indirect discrimination case the employee must first establish a prima facie case of disproportionate adverse impact with valid and significant statistics; merely raising a credible suggestion of possible impact does not shift the burden.
legal_issues: Burden of proof under section 1(3) Equal Pay Act 1970
Indirect sex discrimination and selection of the appropriate statistical pool
TUPE as a material factor unrelated to sex
Harmonisation with Enderby and Barry on equal pay burden of proof

confidence.notes: Leading Court of Appeal analysis of equal pay burden of proof with explicit dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review to block anticipated care proceedings
key_facts: X and Y, parents expecting a baby M, sought judicial review to prevent Gloucestershire County Council commencing emergency protection or care proceedings.
The father was a Schedule 1 offender and both parents had histories of child protection concerns; the council planned care proceedings at birth after abandoning a agreed residential assessment plan.
The parents had previously failed in County Court proceedings and publicised their case in the local press.
Munby J held the local authority had arguable grounds to apply to the Family Proceedings Court and that judicial review was an inappropriate remedy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent application for permission to apply for judicial review and interim injunctive relief to restrain anticipated Children Act proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused, interim relief refused, and judicial review proceedings dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Save in wholly exceptional circumstances, parents should not use the Administrative Court by judicial review to prevent a local authority commencing emergency protection or care proceedings; the proper forum is the Family Proceedings Court or Family Division, judicial review being a remedy of last resort and an unsatisfactory tool for sensitive child protection decisions.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review lies to restrain anticipated Children Act proceedings
Appropriate forum for Article 8 challenges before care proceedings commence
Remedy of last resort and alternative effective remedies
Procedural guidance for fast-tracking such applications in the Administrative Court
index_terms: Re L (Care Proceedings: Human Rights Claims)
P C and S v United Kingdom

linked_authorities.name: Re L (Care Proceedings: Human Rights Claims)
P, C and S v United Kingdom
R v Royal Borough of Kingston-upon-Thames ex p T
R v East Sussex County Council ex p W

confidence.notes: Clear practice guidance judgment with explicit refusal of permission and dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: Allowing Recalde model costs in pipelaying patent trial
key_facts: Following Rockwater's success in the main patent action against Coflexip, only costs remained in dispute.
Rockwater had built a working model of Recalde prior art pipelaying equipment estimated at about £50,000 plus legal supervision costs.
Coflexip argued the model and animations were disproportionate and should be disallowed from the costs award.
The patent dispute concerned high-value relief including potential delivery up of Rockwater's pipelaying vessel Toisa Perseus.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs argument after trial in the Patents Court concerning allowance of demonstrative model and animation expenses.
enrichment.outcome: Full costs of the action awarded to Rockwater, including the model and animation costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where very large sums and potentially catastrophic commercial consequences are at stake in patent litigation, proportionality may justify substantial demonstrative aids such as a working prior art model if they were reasonably incurred and of real use at trial, even if their utility on appeal remains for the appellate court to assess.
legal_issues: Proportionality of litigation costs in high-value patent actions
Allowance of demonstrative models and animations in a costs assessment
Disallowance of costs relating to prior art abandoned before trial

confidence.notes: Short costs-only judgment with clear ruling on the model costs issue.

enrichment.short_title: EAT should hear all redundancy consultation grounds
key_facts: Mrs Vincent, an office manager, was made redundant by M J Gallagher Contractors Ltd and her unfair dismissal claim was rejected by an employment tribunal.
She appealed on six grounds relating to consultation over restructuring, selection criteria, application of criteria, and alternative employment.
At a preliminary EAT hearing the appeal was allowed to proceed on grounds 1 and 5 only; grounds 2, 3, and 4 were dismissed as having no arguable case.
All five live grounds attacked the fairness of the redundancy consultation procedure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision at a preliminary hearing to strike out part of an unfair dismissal appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed with costs; case remitted to the Employment Appeal Tribunal to consider grounds 1 to 5.
enrichment.ratio: Where an unfair dismissal appeal within a comparatively narrow compass turns on the same consultation procedure, an Employment Appeal Tribunal should be cautious before permitting an appeal on some grounds while refusing it on other related grounds at a preliminary hearing unless the split is clearly justified.
legal_issues: Scope of EAT preliminary hearing procedure
When part of an employment appeal may be dismissed as unarguable
Fairness of redundancy selection and consultation procedures
Remittal where related appeal grounds should be heard together

confidence.notes: Short procedural judgment with explicit remittal order.
